sentences.en: My name is Bart de Pau, online Dutch teacher.

sentences.nl: Wanneer gebruiken we wel een lidwoord, en wanneer niet? — Soms gebruiken we in het Nederlands een lidwoord, maar niet in het Engels.
sentences.en: When do we use an article, and when not? — Sometimes we use an article in Dutch, but not in English.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• When use we indeed an article, and when not? — Sometimes use we in the Dutch an article, but not in the English.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence is a question and uses the inverted word order typical of questions in Dutch: "Wanneer gebruiken we..." ("When do we use...").  
• The word "wel" is used for emphasis, meaning 'indeed' or 'actually.'  
• "Lidwoord" means "article" (as in grammatical articles like 'a' or 'the').  
• Example 1: "Wanneer ga je naar huis?" (When are you going home?)  
• Example 2: "Soms eten we pasta, maar niet altijd." (Sometimes we eat pasta, but not always.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Wanneer leren we nieuwe woorden, en wanneer herhalen we?" (When do we learn new words, and when do we review?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch, the use of articles differs from English. For example, "de" and "het" are definite articles, and their use is determined by gender and number, unlike the single "the" in English. This can lead to confusion for Dutch speakers learning English and vice versa.

sentences.nl: Zoals in deze zin.
sentences.en: As in this sentence.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• As in this sentence.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Zoals" is a subordinating conjunction meaning "as" or "like," used to introduce examples or comparisons.  
• "In deze zin" translates to "in this sentence," where "deze" is a demonstrative pronoun meaning "this" and "zin" means "sentence."  
• Word order is standard for a subordinate clause: conjunction + prepositional phrase.  

Extra Examples:  
• Zoals ik al zei. (As I already said.)  
• Zoals je ziet. (As you see.)  
• Zoals verwacht. (As expected.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zoals in dat boek. (As in that book.)

## 4. Culture Note  
• This sentence structure is commonly used in Dutch to provide examples or clarify statements, similar to its use in English.

sentences.nl: Maar andersom kan ook!
sentences.en: But the other way around is also possible!
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• But the other way around is also possible!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Maar" is a conjunction meaning "but."  
• "Andersom" is an adverb meaning "the other way around" or "vice versa."  
• "Kan" is the present tense form of "kunnen," meaning "can" or "is possible."  
• "Ook" means "also" or "too," used here to indicate that the reverse of a previously mentioned situation is possible.

Extra phrases:  
• "Het kan andersom ook." (It can be the other way around too.)  
• "Andersom werkt het niet." (The other way around, it doesn't work.)  
• "Zij kan het andersom ook." (She can do it the other way around too.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Je kunt het probleem andersom bekijken." (You can look at the problem the other way around.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch conversations, "andersom" is often used to express flexibility in situations or to suggest considering an alternative perspective, showing the Dutch appreciation for pragmatism and problem-solving.

sentences.nl: In deze les oefenen we Nederlandse zinnen, met de grammatica van #dutchgrammar les 21, over het lidwoord.
sentences.en: In this lesson, we practice Dutch sentences with the grammar from #dutchgrammar lesson 21, about the article.

sentences.nl: Marieke en Gianluca lopen naar het station.
sentences.en: Marieke and Gianluca are walking to the station.

sentences.nl: Het is al laat.
sentences.en: It is already late.

sentences.nl: Bedankt dat je me naar het station brengt.
sentences.en: Thank you for taking me to the station.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Thanks that you me to the station bring.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Bedankt dat je me naar het station brengt" uses a subordinate clause introduced by "dat," which causes the verb "brengt" to move to the end of the clause.  
• "Brengt" is the present tense of "brengen" (to bring). The verb is conjugated according to the subject "je" (you).  
• "Naar" is a preposition meaning "to," commonly used to indicate direction or destination.

Extra phrases/sentences:  
• "Ik ben blij dat je er bent." (I am happy that you are here.)  
• "Zij zegt dat ze het boek leest." (She says that she is reading the book.)  
• "Kun je me naar huis brengen?" (Can you bring me home?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Dank je dat je de deur voor me opent." (Thank you for opening the door for me.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, it is common to thank someone (using "bedankt" or "dank je") for small favors or acts of kindness, reflecting a culture of politeness and appreciation.

sentences.nl: ‘Geen probleem’, zegt Gianluca.
sentences.en: "No problem," says Gianluca.

sentences.nl: Ik vind het wel gezellig.
sentences.en: I think it's cozy.

sentences.nl: En jij bent een mooie vrouw!
sentences.en: And you are a beautiful woman!

sentences.nl: Nou nou…
sentences.en: Well, well...

sentences.nl: Marieke moet blozen.
sentences.en: Marieke has to blush.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Marieke must blush.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Moet" is the present tense, third-person singular form of "moeten," meaning "must" or "have to." It indicates obligation or necessity.  
• "Blozen" is an infinitive verb meaning "to blush." In Dutch, when using modal verbs like "moeten," the main verb stays in the infinitive form.

Examples:  
• Hij moet werken. (He must work.)  
• Zij moet studeren voor het examen. (She must study for the exam.)  
• We moeten vroeg opstaan. (We have to get up early.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Lisa moet lachen. (Lisa must laugh.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, directness is often valued, and expressions like "moet blozen" might indicate a straightforward acknowledgment of emotions in social settings.

sentences.nl: Ze vindt de aandacht van Gianluca wel leuk.
sentences.en: She quite likes the attention from Gianluca.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• She finds the attention of Gianluca indeed nice.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Ze vindt" is in the present tense and means "she finds." The verb "vinden" (to find) is used here to express an opinion.  
• "De aandacht van Gianluca" translates to "the attention of Gianluca." The structure "de aandacht van [name]" shows possession.  
• "Wel leuk" is an informal way to say "indeed nice" or "rather nice," with "wel" adding emphasis or confirmation. 

Examples:  
- "Ik vind de muziek wel mooi." (I find the music indeed beautiful.)  
- "Hij vindt het eten wel lekker." (He finds the food indeed tasty.)  
- "Ze vindt het boek wel interessant." (She finds the book indeed interesting.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Ze vindt de nieuwe film wel spannend." (She finds the new movie indeed exciting.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, using "wel" in a sentence can soften or make a statement more polite, often used to express a mild or moderate level of enthusiasm or agreement.

sentences.nl: Vertel eens iets over jezelf.
sentences.en: Tell me something about yourself.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Tell once something about yourself.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Vertel eens" uses the imperative form of the verb "vertellen" (to tell), with "eens" softening the command to make it more of a suggestion or polite request.  
• "Iets" is an indefinite pronoun meaning "something."  
• "Over jezelf" means "about yourself," where "over" is a preposition and "jezelf" is a reflexive pronoun.

Extra Examples:  
• "Kijk eens naar de sterren." (Look at the stars.)  
• "Zeg eens wat je denkt." (Say what you think.)  
• "Ik wil iets over het boek vertellen." (I want to tell something about the book.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Vertel eens wat je gisteren hebt gedaan." (Tell me what you did yesterday.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, asking someone to "vertel eens iets over jezelf" is a common way to encourage someone to share personal information in a relaxed setting, often used in social or networking situations.

sentences.nl: Eh, wat wil je weten? — Waarom ben je in Nederland? — Voor mijn werk.
sentences.en: Eh, what do you want to know? — Why are you in the Netherlands? — For my work.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Eh, what want you know? — Why are you in Netherlands? — For my work.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Eh" is an informal filler word similar to "uh" or "well" in English.  
• "Wat wil je weten?" uses the structure for asking questions in Dutch, where the verb "wil" (want) precedes the subject "je" (you).  
• "Waarom ben je in Nederland?" uses "ben" as the present tense of "zijn" (to be) and the question word "waarom" (why).  
• "Voor mijn werk" uses "voor" to indicate purpose or reason.

Examples:  
• "Wat kan ik voor je doen?" (What can I do for you?)  
• "Waarom ga je weg?" (Why are you leaving?)  
• "Ik ben hier voor mijn studie." (I am here for my studies.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Eh, hoe laat begint de vergadering?" (Uh, what time does the meeting start?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• "Eh" is commonly used in Dutch informal speech to pause or think, similar to "um" or "uh" in English. It's not considered impolite and is often used in casual conversation.

sentences.nl: Oh ja? Wat doe je? — Ik ben dokter.
sentences.en: Oh really? What do you do? — I am a doctor.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Oh yes? What do you do? — I am doctor.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Oh ja?" is an informal way to express mild surprise or interest, similar to "Oh really?" in English.  
• "Wat doe je?" uses the verb "doen" (to do) in the present tense, structured as "Wat + verb + subject?" This is a common question format in Dutch.  
• "Ik ben dokter" uses "ben" which is the first-person singular form of "zijn" (to be). No article is used before professions in Dutch, unlike in English where "a" or "an" is required.

• Extra Examples:  
  - "Wat lees je?" (What are you reading?)  
  - "Ik ben leraar." (I am a teacher.)  
  - "Oh ja? Heb je dat gezien?" (Oh really? Did you see that?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Oh ja? Waar woon je? — Ik woon in Amsterdam." (Oh really? Where do you live? — I live in Amsterdam.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, it is common to ask about someone's profession shortly after meeting them, as careers are often seen as a significant part of one's identity.

sentences.nl: Dokter? — Wauw…
sentences.en: Doctor? — Wow…

sentences.nl: Ik ben cardioloog in het AMC.
sentences.en: I am a cardiologist at the AMC.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• I am cardiologist in the AMC.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Ik ben" means "I am," using the verb "zijn" (to be) in the first person singular.  
• "Cardioloog" is a noun meaning "cardiologist." In Dutch, professions typically don't need an article unless specified.  
• "In het" means "in the," using the definite article "het" for a neuter noun.  
• "AMC" refers to a specific place, the Academic Medical Center in Amsterdam.

• Extra examples:  
  – "Ik ben leraar in de basisschool." (I am a teacher in the primary school.)  
  – "Zij is ingenieur bij Philips." (She is an engineer at Philips.)  
  – "Hij werkt als verpleegkundige in het ziekenhuis." (He works as a nurse in the hospital.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Zij is tandarts in Utrecht." (She is a dentist in Utrecht.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The AMC, or Academic Medical Center, is a well-known hospital and research facility in Amsterdam, often associated with the University of Amsterdam. It's a prestigious place to work, especially for medical professionals.

sentences.nl: Je bent cardioloog…
sentences.en: You are a cardiologist…

sentences.nl: Oh… Ik ben onder de indruk.
sentences.en: Oh... I am impressed.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Oh… I am under the impression.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The phrase "onder de indruk" is an idiomatic expression meaning "impressed."  
• "Onder" is a preposition meaning "under," and "de indruk" means "the impression." Together, they create the idiomatic meaning.  
• The verb "ben" is the first-person singular present tense of "zijn" (to be).  
• Example sentences:  
  - Hij is onder de indruk van haar talent. (He is impressed by her talent.)  
  - Wij waren onder de indruk van het concert. (We were impressed by the concert.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij is onder de indruk van zijn presentatie. (She is impressed by his presentation.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, expressing being "onder de indruk" can be a sincere compliment, often used in professional or formal situations to acknowledge someone's effort or talent.

sentences.nl: En je bent Italiaan? — Ja, ik ben Italiaan,, maar ik ben ook Amerikaan.
sentences.en: And you are Italian? — Yes, I am Italian, but I am also American.

sentences.nl: Heb je 2 nationaliteiten? — Ja, inderdaad.
sentences.en: Do you have 2 nationalities? — Yes, indeed.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Have you 2 nationalities? — Yes, indeed.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence starts with "Heb je," which is an inversion typical in yes/no questions, where the verb comes before the subject.  
• "Inderdaad" is an adverb meaning "indeed" or "certainly," used for emphasis or confirmation.  
• Example sentences:  
  - Heb je het boek gelezen? (Have you read the book?)  
  - Is het koud buiten? — Ja, inderdaad. (Is it cold outside? — Yes, indeed.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Heb je al gegeten? — Ja, inderdaad. (Have you eaten yet? — Yes, indeed.)

## 4. Culture Note  
• In the Netherlands, it's common for people to have dual nationalities due to the country's history of immigration and international connections. This sentence could be part of a casual conversation exploring one's background.

sentences.nl: Mijn vader is Italiaan, en mijn moeder komt uit de Verenigde Staten.
sentences.en: My father is Italian, and my mother is from the United States.

sentences.nl: En wat zijn je hobby’s? — Mijn hobby’s…
sentences.en: And what are your hobbies? — My hobbies…
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• And what are your hobbies? — My hobbies...

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence begins with "En" (And), commonly used in Dutch to continue a conversation or connect thoughts.  
• "Wat zijn" is the question structure for "What are," utilizing the verb "zijn" (to be) with "wat" (what).  
• "je hobby’s" means "your hobbies," where "je" is the informal possessive pronoun for "your."  
• Dutch uses an apostrophe before the "s" in pluralizing words ending in a vowel sound to maintain readability.

Extra Phrases:  
• Wat zijn je plannen voor het weekend? (What are your plans for the weekend?)  
• En wat doe je voor werk? (And what do you do for work?)  
• Mijn plannen zijn nog niet zeker. (My plans are not certain yet.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• En wat zijn je favoriete boeken? (And what are your favorite books?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch-speaking regions, talking about hobbies is a common way to engage in small talk and get to know someone better. It's a friendly way to find common interests.

sentences.nl: Ehh… voetbal kijken en koffie drinken…
sentences.en: Uh… watching football and drinking coffee…

sentences.nl: Koffie drinken? — Koffie drinken met een mooie vrouw…
sentences.en: Drink coffee? — Drink coffee with a beautiful woman…

sentences.nl: Marieke moet lachen…
sentences.en: Marieke has to laugh…
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Marieke must laugh…

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Moet" is the present tense of "moeten," meaning "must" or "have to." It indicates obligation or necessity.  
• In Dutch, the modal verb (e.g., "moet") is typically followed by the infinitive form of the main verb (e.g., "lachen").  
• Examples:  
  - "Ik moet werken." (I must work.)  
  - "Zij moet studeren." (She must study.)  
  - "Wij moeten vertrekken." (We must leave.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Jasper moet huilen." (Jasper must cry.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Laughter is a universal human expression, and in Dutch culture, humor is often dry and straightforward. The sentence suggests an involuntary need to laugh, which could be due to something genuinely funny or awkward.

sentences.nl: Ah, natuurlijk, zoals een echte Italiaan.
sentences.en: Ah, of course, like a true Italian.

sentences.nl: En jij bent docent Nederlands? — Ja, ik ben docent Nederlands in Rotterdam.
sentences.en: And you are a Dutch teacher? — Yes, I am a Dutch teacher in Rotterdam.

sentences.nl: Geef je ook privéles? — Ja, ik geef soms privéles bij expats thuis.
sentences.en: Do you also give private lessons? — Yes, I sometimes give private lessons at expats' homes.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• "Geef je ook privéles?" — "Do you also give private lessons?"  
• "Ja, ik geef soms privéles bij expats thuis." — "Yes, I give sometimes private lessons at expats' home."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Geef je" is a question structure where the verb comes first, followed by the subject ("je"). This inversion is typical in Dutch questions.  
• "Ook" means "also," used to add information.  
• "Soms" means "sometimes" and typically precedes the verb in sentences.  
• "Bij expats thuis" means "at expats' home," where "bij" is a preposition indicating location.  
• Extra phrases:  
  - "Werk je ook op zaterdag?" (Do you also work on Saturday?)  
  - "Ik ga soms naar de bibliotheek." (I sometimes go to the library.)  
  - "Zij woont bij haar ouders thuis." (She lives at her parents' home.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Geef je ook les aan kinderen?" (Do you also teach children?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, private lessons or tutoring are common among expats who seek to learn Dutch or other subjects tailored to their needs at home.

sentences.nl: Je bent echt mooi.
sentences.en: You are really beautiful.

sentences.nl: Wil je mij ook privéles geven? — Eh… heb je een vriendin? — Niet hier.
sentences.en: Do you also want to give me private lessons? — Uh… do you have a girlfriend? — Not here.

sentences.nl: Niet hier? — Wat bedoel je? — Je hebt zeker een vriendin in ItaliÎ…
sentences.en: Not here? — What do you mean? — You certainly have a girlfriend in Italy…
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Not here? — What mean you? — You have certainly a girlfriend in Italy...

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Niet hier?" uses "niet" for negation, placed before the adverb "hier."  
• "Wat bedoel je?" is a common way to ask for clarification, with "bedoel" as the verb meaning "to mean," followed by the subject "je" (you).  
• "Je hebt zeker een vriendin in Italië…" uses "zeker" to mean "certainly" or "surely," placed after the verb "hebt" (have). The sentence implies suspicion or accusation with the trailing ellipsis.

Examples:  
- "Niet nu?" (Not now?)  
- "Wat zeg je?" (What are you saying?)  
- "Hij heeft zeker een geheim." (He certainly has a secret.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Zeker weten dat hij komt?" (Are you sure that he is coming?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• None

sentences.nl: Hmmmm….
sentences.en: Hmmmm....

sentences.nl: Eh… nee, dat bedoel ik niet…

sentences.nl: Ik snap het verschil niet… vriend of vriendin…
sentences.en: I don't understand the difference… friend or girlfriend…
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• I understand the difference not… friend or girlfriend…

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Snap" is an informal verb meaning "understand." It's often used in conversational Dutch.  
• The phrase "het verschil" means "the difference," with "het" as the definite article for neuter nouns.  
• Word order in Dutch often places the direct object before the negation, as in "het verschil niet."

Extra Examples:  
• "Ik snap het niet." (I don't understand it.)  
• "Begrijp je het verschil?" (Do you understand the difference?)  
• "Hij snapt het probleem wel." (He does understand the problem.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Ik snap de grap niet." (I don't understand the joke.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch, "vriend" can mean both "friend" and "boyfriend," while "vriendin" can mean both "female friend" and "girlfriend." Context is key to understanding which meaning is intended.

sentences.nl: Jaja…
sentences.en: Yeah, yeah...

sentences.nl: Voor Marieke is het een afknapper.
sentences.en: For Marieke, it's a turn-off.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• For Marieke is it a turn-off.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The word "afknapper" is a noun that means "turn-off" or "disappointment," commonly used to describe something that negatively changes one's view or experience.  
• The sentence follows a subject-verb-inversion structure due to the prepositional phrase "Voor Marieke" at the beginning. This is common in Dutch when the sentence starts with something other than the subject.  
• "Het" is a pronoun that refers to a previously mentioned or understood situation or thing.

• Extra phrases:  
  - "Voor hem is het een uitdaging." (For him, it is a challenge.)  
  - "Voor de kinderen is het een avontuur." (For the children, it is an adventure.)  
  - "Voor haar was het een verrassing." (For her, it was a surprise.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Voor ons is het een groot probleem." (For us, it is a big problem.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, straightforwardness is valued, and expressing one's feelings about situations, such as calling something an "afknapper," is common and generally accepted.

sentences.nl: Ze zijn bijna bij het station.
sentences.en: They are almost at the station.

sentences.nl: ‘Over 2 minuten gaat mijn trein’, zegt Marieke.
sentences.en: "My train leaves in 2 minutes," says Marieke.

sentences.nl: Ik moet rennen… doei!!!!
sentences.en: I have to run… bye!!!!
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• I must run… bye!!!!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Ik moet" is a simple present tense construction meaning "I must" or "I have to," indicating obligation or necessity.  
• "Rennen" is the infinitive form of the verb "to run." In Dutch, the infinitive follows modal verbs like "moet."  
• "Doei" is an informal way to say "bye" in Dutch.

- "Ik moet studeren voor het examen." (I must study for the exam.)
- "Hij moet morgen vroeg opstaan." (He must get up early tomorrow.)
- "Doei, tot snel!" (Bye, see you soon!)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik moet koken… tot later! (I have to cook… see you later!)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• "Doei" is commonly used among friends and in informal settings. In more formal situations, you might say "tot ziens" (goodbye).

sentences.nl: Marieke rent naar de trein.
sentences.en: Marieke runs to the train.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Marieke runs to the train.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The verb "rent" is the third-person singular form of "rennen" (to run), in the present tense.  
• "Naar" is a preposition meaning "to" or "towards," indicating direction.  
• Word order in the sentence follows the Subject-Verb-Object pattern, which is typical in Dutch for simple present tense sentences.

• Examples:  
  - "Hij loopt naar het park." (He walks to the park.)  
  - "Zij fietst naar school." (She bikes to school.)  
  - "We gaan naar het museum." (We are going to the museum.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Pieter zwemt naar de overkant van het meer." (Pieter swims to the other side of the lake.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• None.

sentences.nl: Gianluca blijft achter.
sentences.en: Gianluca stays behind.

sentences.nl: Hmmm, dan ga ik maar een kopje koffie drinken.
sentences.en: Hmm, then I'll just have a cup of coffee.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Hmmm, then go I just a cup coffee drink.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The word "dan" (then) is used to indicate a subsequent action or decision.  
• "Maar" here functions as a softener, often translating to "just" or "only," implying a casual or modest action.  
• The phrase "een kopje koffie drinken" (to drink a cup of coffee) is common in Dutch, where "kopje" is a diminutive form of "kop" (cup).  
• Example Sentences:  
  - "Dan ga ik naar huis." (Then I am going home.)  
  - "Zij neemt maar één koekje." (She takes just one cookie.)  
  - "Wil je een kopje thee drinken?" (Do you want to drink a cup of tea?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Dan ga ik maar een wandeling maken." (Then I will just go for a walk.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, drinking coffee is a common social activity, often used as an excuse to take a break or have a chat. The use of "maar" in this context suggests a casual, unplanned decision, which is a typical way to express spontaneity.

sentences.nl: Dat was de les van vandaag.
sentences.en: That was today's lesson.

sentences.nl: Ben je al abonnee van mijn kanaal op Youtube? — Als je op abonneren [subscribe] klikt,, dan krijg je elke week nieuwe lessen!
sentences.en: Are you already a subscriber to my channel on YouTube? — If you click subscribe, you'll get new lessons every week!
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Are you already subscriber of my channel on YouTube? — If you on subscribe click, then get you every week new lessons!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Ben je" is an inversion used for questions, where the verb "ben" (are) comes before the subject "je" (you).  
• "Als je op abonneren klikt" uses "als" (if) to introduce a conditional clause, followed by the verb "klikt" (click) which is in the present tense. "Op" is a preposition meaning "on" used with "klikken" (to click).  
• "Dan krijg je" is a main clause that follows a conditional clause, using "krijg" (get) in present tense.  
• Examples:  
  - "Ben je klaar om te gaan?" (Are you ready to go?)  
  - "Als het regent, neem ik een paraplu mee." (If it rains, I take an umbrella with me.)  
  - "Klik op de knop om door te gaan." (Click on the button to continue.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Ben je al abonnee van de nieuwsbrief?" (Are you already a subscriber of the newsletter?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• YouTube is widely used in the Netherlands for educational content, entertainment, and vlogging. Many Dutch content creators encourage subscriptions for regular updates, similar to creators worldwide.
